name: Miracles as Signs of the Coming Kingdom
path: New Testament Studies: Life and Doctrine in Christ
The Gospels and the Life of Christ

objectives.text: Retell the account of Jesus giving sight to a man born blind
Retell the account of Jesus walking on the water and name what the disciples said about him afterward
Recall how Jesus fed more than five thousand people with a boy's five loaves and two fish and had food left over
Describe how Jesus raised Lazarus from the tomb and what Jesus said about himself before doing it
Summarize two reasons the Gospels give for Jesus' miracles, his compassion for people and his revealing of who he is
Explain what Jesus calming the storm shows about his authority over wind and sea
Distinguish a miracle as God's direct work above ordinary means from a magic trick that relies on deception or hidden technique
Explain how Jesus used the healing of the paralyzed man to show his authority to forgive sins
Explain how Jesus pointed to his miracles to show John the Baptist that Isaiah's promises of the coming kingdom were being fulfilled
Analyze how Jesus' healings and nature miracles reverse effects of the fall such as sickness, hunger, and death
Analyze the signs in John's Gospel by tracing how each one reveals Jesus' glory and serves John's stated purpose for writing
Explain how Jesus' casting out of demons demonstrates that the kingdom of God has come and that Satan is being overthrown
Explain the transfiguration as a preview of the King's glory and connect it to Jesus' promise that some would see the kingdom come in power
Explain why Jesus refused to perform signs on demand and how the Gospels relate miracles to faith
Classify Jesus' miracles as nature miracles, healings, exorcisms, and raisings from the dead and explain what each category reveals about his kingdom
Compare Jesus' miracles with miracles performed through Moses, Elijah, and Elisha to show how the Gospels present Jesus as greater than the prophets
Evaluate the responses of the Pharisees, the crowds, and the disciples to Jesus' miracles and what those responses reveal about unbelief and faith
Evaluate common naturalistic objections to the Gospel miracles and defend their historicity using eyewitness testimony and the public nature of the events
Explain the Reformed position that miracles chiefly attested Christ and the apostolic message and relate it to the tradition's teaching that former ways of revealing God's will have ceased
Compose a theological argument presenting Jesus' miracles as a foretaste of the new heavens and new earth, drawing on Old Testament promises and the Bible's closing vision

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies in the early-grade retellings, the purposes of miracles, the calming of the storm, the paralytic, restoration of creation, John's signs, exorcisms, the transfiguration, categorization, responses to miracles, historicity, and the new-creation synthesis. Rewrote observe and name stems as retell or describe so they are observable. Recast magic versus miracle as a distinction grounded in the tradition's definition of a miracle (WCF 5.3). Added competencies that were missing: Jesus' miracles as fulfillment of Isaiah's kingdom promises (Matthew 11:2-6), why Jesus refused signs on demand and how miracles relate to faith, comparison with the miracles of Moses, Elijah, and Elisha, and the Reformed view of miracles as attesting the apostolic message. Tied exorcisms to Christ's kingly office (WSC Q26). Replaced whole-account references with verse ranges and added passages where the objectives rest on them. Kept Lazarus as a miracle account and left the resurrection narrative itself to the Passion Week sibling.
